THOUGHT: This 70-year-old man presents with a classic parkinsonian motor syndrome: asymmetric (left-dominant) resting tremor, mild rigidity in upper extremities, hypomimia (reduced facial expression), and hypophonia (soft, monotonous speech). These features are highly characteristic of Parkinson disease (PD), especially given the progressive, insidious onset over one year. The absence of red flags—such as early falls, severe autonomic dysfunction (e.g., orthostatic hypotension), prominent cerebellar signs, vertical gaze palsy, or marked symmetric onset—makes atypical parkinsonism (e.g., multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy) less likely. His memory complaints—forgetfulness with financial mismanagement—are consistent with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) associated with PD (i.e., Parkinson disease–mild cognitive impairment, PD-MCI), which commonly precedes or co-occurs with motor symptoms; this is distinct from Alzheimer disease, where memory impairment is typically more prominent early on and motor signs are absent. The brain MRI shows only mild age-appropriate atrophy, no structural lesions, vascular changes, or hippocampal atrophy suggestive of AD or other dementias. Normal thyroid function and CBC rule out metabolic or hematologic causes of tremor or cognitive change. His alcohol intake (1–2 beers nightly) is modest and unlikely to cause progressive parkinsonism or significant cognitive decline; cigar smoking history is not strongly linked to PD (though some epidemiologic data suggest reduced risk). Family history of maternal schizophrenia is not associated with increased PD risk and does not alter the neurodegenerative interpretation. Overall, the constellation of asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia (inferred from difficulty reading—likely due to tremor + micrographia/bradykinesia—and task instability), rigidity, hypomimia, and hypophonia, plus progressive course and absence of alternative explanations, fulfills clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson disease (e.g., MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for PD). Cognitive changes are best viewed as part of the PD spectrum rather than a separate primary dementia diagnosis at this stage.

DIAGNOSIS: Parkinson disease
